newsitem.title: USA: Airline back in business after Clinton stops strike.
newsitem.headline: Airline back in business after Clinton stops strike.

text.p: American Airlines rushed on Saturday to put its planes back in the air and passengers in its seats after President Bill Clinton cut short a pilots' strike just minutes after it shut the carrier down.

The airline offered huge discounts on weekend flights in a bid to attract passengers who had rebooked with its rivals to avoid getting caught by a strike, and delighted passengers boarded planes after anxious waits of several hours.

Clinton stepped in shortly after midnight EST Friday (0500 GMT on Saturday), minutes after union leaders ordered all of American's 9,300 pilots to walk off the job because five days of intense negotiations with management had failed to bring agreement on a new four-year labor contract.
Clinton established a Presidential Emergency Board, which effectively postpones any possible strike at the nation's second-largest airline for another 60 days.
American officials said they were delighted Clinton had halted the 24-minute strike, which would have cost the economy as much as $200 million a day and the airline about $30 million per day.
The move upset many of the airline's pilots, while bringing huge relief at airports across the country.

"I am very happy he intervened. No worries," Emily Ghio, a 16-year-old from California, said as she hugged her parents and then boarded an American flight from Los Angeles to Boston to compete in a fencing competition at the Junior Olympics.
Just minutes earlier, as pilots at the airport marched in single file to set up picket lines, Ghio and hundreds of other passengers thought they were going to be stranded.
But Clinton's announcement was quickly relayed across the country and virtually all scheduled flights were resumed.
In a bid to regain passengers who had jumped ship as the strike loomed, American quickly announced a series of sales and promotions for passengers and cargo shippers.

They included discounts of up to 50 percent on 21-day excursion fares and 40 percent on portions of tour packages, a doubling of frequent flier mile credits and 45 percent discounts for cargo customers.

Although the strike lasted only a few minutes, American lost tens of millions of dollars in recent days as passengers rebooked their flights for the long Presidents Day holiday weekend and virtually ignored the carrier as they made travel plans for the next month and beyond.
